title: Soft-Boiled Eggs
subtitle: Jammy whites and a warm, flowing yolk
excerpt: Boiling an egg sounds simple, but the difference between a flowing yolk and a chalky one is under a minute. These timings make it reliable every time.
sourceNotes: Standard British soft-boiled egg technique. Timings based on a large egg (65 g) straight from the fridge, lowered into already-boiling water.

glossaryTerms.definition: To maintain liquid at a temperature just below boiling, around 85 to 95 °C, with small bubbles rising steadily rather than a full rolling boil.

content.text: A soft-boiled egg asks very little of you: a pan of boiling water, a timer, and the discipline to not wander off. The result ranges from a barely-set, flowing yolk at 4 minutes to a gently firmed jammy centre at 6, and the difference between them is a matter of taste rather than error. Knowing which you want, and trusting the timer, is the whole skill.
What you need

items.prepNote: large, taken straight from the fridge

content.text: Fill a saucepan with water deep enough to cover the eggs by 2 cm and bring to a full rolling boil over high heat.
Lower the eggs in gently with a slotted spoon and start the timer immediately. Reduce to a steady simmer.
Cook for 4 to 6 minutes to your preferred set, then lift out and serve in egg cups with a pinch of sea salt.
Boil and time
Fill the saucepan with enough water to cover the
eggs

by at least 2 cm and bring it to a full rolling boil over high heat. Once boiling, lower the eggs in gently with the slotted spoon, lower them, do not drop them, or the shells will crack on impact. Start the timer the moment the eggs are in the water.
Reduce the heat slightly so the water settles to a steady
simmer
rather than a vigorous boil, the eggs bounce less and crack less. Cook for the time that matches what you want (see the timing reference below).
Timing reference
These timings are for large eggs (around 65 g) straight from the fridge. Room-temperature eggs cook faster by about 30 to 45 seconds.
4 minutes: white barely set, yolk completely liquid and warm
5 minutes: white fully set, yolk runny and flowing freely
6 minutes: white fully set, yolk jammy at the edges, still flowing in the centre, the sweet spot for most people
Lift and serve

When the timer goes, lift the eggs out with the slotted spoon and serve immediately in egg cups. A soft-boiled egg loses heat quickly in the shell, so have your cups, toast, and anything else ready before the timer sounds. Tap the top with a teaspoon and peel away the cap of shell. Season the yolk with a pinch of sea salt.
Troubleshooter

Shell cracking in the water: the egg went in too cold or was lowered in too fast. Fridge-cold eggs need to be placed in gently. A small pinhole in the rounded end with a pin before cooking allows air to escape and reduces cracking, though most people don't bother.

Yolk firmer than expected: the eggs were at room temperature, or the water was at a more vigorous boil than intended. Note your conditions and subtract 30 seconds next time. Egg size also matters, small eggs (55 g) cook noticeably faster than large.
Where this dish lives

The soft-boiled egg in an egg cup is one of the most recognisable images of the British breakfast table, as much a fixture as the teapot and the marmalade. It appears in children's books, wartime ration recipes, and on every hotel breakfast menu. It is one of those preparations that seems almost too simple to merit a recipe, until you overcook it and end up with a chalky yolk and a sulphurous smell. With the right timing, it needs nothing but an egg cup and a little salt.
